table.brief: Bill of materials: Part number (like RC0402FR-0710KL) / Description (long) / Qty / Unit price / Supplier

conditions.browser: Chromium (Playwright build), macOS system fonts, deviceScaleFactor 1

candidates.name: d1r1B
candidates.idea: Test a scrolling compromise with a wider description than B. It should reduce wrapping of specifications and package codes while keeping purchasing fields substantially closer than in C.
candidates.label: gold

lineInfo.text: MHz, 64 KB flash, 20 KB RAM, LQFP-48

whys: Identifiers stay whole and the consistently two-line descriptions make rows easy to scan. The initial viewport cuts through descriptions and leaves quantity, price and supplier offscreen; a few values and units also fall on separate lines.

The full table has consistently two-line descriptions and an even row rhythm. Its greater width puts more of each description and all quantity, price and supplier data beyond the initial viewport, increasing horizontal travel.

Descriptions fit in two lines and the uniform row heights make scanning easy; identifiers and purchasing fields remain intact. Its greater width requires substantial horizontal travel, and the first view cuts through descriptions.

candidates.name: d1r2A
candidates.idea: Test a viewport-fitting compromise that preserves complete prices while distributing the remaining space between identifiers, descriptions and suppliers. Compare whether the gain in price readability outweighs additional wrapping elsewhere.
candidates.label: bad

whys: All columns are visible and prices stay whole, but part numbers, supplier names and even headers fragment across lines. Tall rows and a very narrow supplier column make lookup and continuous reading difficult.

Quantity and prices are legible and the wider description column improves on A and E. Part numbers still fragment, and the very narrow supplier column breaks names into tiny pieces, making identification difficult.
All columns are visible and prices stay together, but part numbers, descriptions and especially supplier names fragment severely. Tall rows and broken headers make lookup slow.

candidates.name: d2r2B
candidates.idea: Explore a wider scrolling layout that gives technical descriptions more room and may reduce awkward breaks and row heights, at the cost of additional horizontal travel.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Cortex-M3 stays together, improving on B, while most rows remain compact. The microcontroller description still runs to three lines, and the initial viewport cuts through the description column.

The full table has clear grouping and mostly two-line descriptions. On the phone, however, descriptions run beyond the initial viewport and all three transactional columns are offscreen; reading across a row takes more scrolling than in B.

Part numbers and prices stay intact, and most descriptions occupy two lines. The microcontroller description needs three, while the initial viewport cuts through the description and hides the purchasing columns.

candidates.name: d3r1C
candidates.idea: Test a middle-width scrolling layout: give descriptions substantially more breathing room than d3r0B while keeping purchasing fields closer than in d3r0C.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Most descriptions occupy two lines and the compact rows scan well, but Cortex-M3 breaks at the hyphen and the longest description needs three lines. The first viewport cuts through descriptions and hides the remaining columns.

The full table is compact and orderly, with intact identifiers and mostly two-line descriptions. The initial viewport cuts through descriptions, and the microcontroller description breaks Cortex-M3 across lines.

The table is compact and its identifiers remain intact, but the microcontroller's Cortex-M3 designation breaks across lines. The initial viewport shows only part of the description and none of the purchasing columns.

The initial view contains complete part numbers and descriptions, making identification practical before scrolling. Narrow descriptions create three- and four-line rows and separate some values from their units; quantity, price and supplier remain offscreen.

Identifiers, prices and suppliers stay whole, and the complete description column is visible initially. Descriptions are somewhat narrow and create several four-line rows, while quantity, price and supplier require scrolling.

The initial view contains the part numbers and nearly all of each description, with less horizontal travel to the other fields. Three- and four-line descriptions make rows tall, and breaks such as 1 / μF interrupt technical units.

candidates.name: contrast
candidates.idea: Near-equal widths fit the viewport but give unnecessary space to quantity while splitting part numbers, prices, supplier names and descriptions. Equal treatment ignores their different content and lookup roles.
candidates.label: bad

whys: Equal widths give excess space to quantity while splitting part numbers, prices, descriptions and supplier names. The resulting long rows make even a short BOM laborious to scan.
The grid remains intact, but part numbers, descriptions, suppliers and even prices break across lines. Tall rows and largely empty quantity cells make lookup and comparison laborious.
Equal widths give quantity unnecessary room while splitting part numbers, words and even prices. Extremely tall rows make cross-column comparison laborious despite the table fitting on screen.

Part number, description and quantity are visible together initially, and identifiers and prices remain whole. The narrow description column breaks technical phrases across many short lines, producing tall rows and substantial empty space in neighboring cells.

Part numbers, complete descriptions and quantities are visible together initially, and the shorter scroll reaches price and supplier. The narrow description column creates tall rows and awkward breaks in technical phrases; the price header also wraps.

Part number, description and quantity appear together initially, and the remaining columns require less scrolling. Narrow descriptions produce up to six lines and split technical designations; the price header also wraps.
Like F, this fragments identifiers, prices and ordinary words while leaving unused space in quantity cells. Its slightly narrower columns produce still more wrapping and a taller table.
The equal narrow columns split identifiers, words, supplier names and prices. Long description stacks stretch the rows while the quantity column contains extensive unused space.
The narrow equal columns fragment identifiers, descriptions and prices, with very tall rows and large unused areas beside the text. The small reduction in width offers no practical reading benefit.

d1.purpose: Identify and procure the components needed for a prototype controller board.
tasks: Look up a part number and find its description, quantity, price, and supplier.
Compare quantities and unit prices across components.
Read each description to verify specifications and package details.
relations: Each row represents one component; its part number, specifications, quantity, unit price, and supplier belong together.
Quantity and unit price are related purchasing facts, while the description distinguishes parts with similar functions.
roles: The header names five fields; the seven body rows have equal structural status.
Part number is the primary identifier, description carries variable-length technical detail, and the remaining columns support purchasing.
keep_whole: Part numbers and supplier names where space permits.
Quantities, prices, model names, package codes, and compact specification values such as 0.1 µF.
may_wrap: Descriptions at natural word and comma boundaries.
Multiword supplier names and column headers when necessary.
same_scale: Use consistent widths within each column and give the compact quantity and price fields appropriately compact space.
Give identifiers and supplier names enough space for their longest entries in scrolling layouts; descriptions deserve more space because they contain much more text.
d1.h_vs_v: A viewport-fitting table exposes all fields together but forces identifiers, prices, and supplier names to break and makes rows tall. Scrolling preserves those units and allows shorter rows, at the cost of hiding later fields initially; a wider description further reduces vertical reading at the cost of more scrolling.

d2.purpose: Document the parts and purchasing details needed to assemble a prototype controller board.
tasks: Identify a component by part number or description.
Check the quantity and unit price for each component.
Find the supplier and compare purchasing details across rows.
relations: Each row connects one part number to its description, quantity, unit price, and supplier.
Descriptions distinguish component characteristics; quantities and prices support purchasing decisions.
roles: The header names five fields; each subsequent row represents one BOM item.
Part numbers are lookup identifiers, descriptions carry technical detail, and the remaining columns provide purchasing information.
keep_whole: Part numbers, numeric values with units, prices, and supplier names should remain intact where space permits.
The longest part number needs 186px including padding and border; the longest supplier name needs 154px.
may_wrap: Descriptions may wrap at natural word and punctuation boundaries.
Multiword headers and supplier names may wrap at spaces when necessary.
same_scale: Quantity and unit price are compact numerical fields, though price needs more width.
Part number and supplier both benefit from enough width to preserve identifiers and names.
d2.h_vs_v: A fitting table exposes every field at once but forces identifiers and supplier names to split and makes rows tall. Scrolling can preserve those lookup units; additional description width trades more horizontal travel for fewer lines.

d3.purpose: List the components needed to build a prototype controller board and provide purchasing details.
tasks: Identify a component by part number or description.
Read the required quantity and unit price.
Find the supplier and compare purchasing details across rows.
relations: Each row connects one part number and its technical description to a quantity, unit price and supplier.
Technical values and package codes in a description qualify that row's component.
Unit prices apply per component; quantities are counts, not prices or totals.
roles: The header row labels five fields with distinct lookup and purchasing roles.
Part numbers act as identifiers even though no row-header column is declared.
Descriptions distinguish components and their specifications; quantity and price are compact numeric fields; supplier names identify sources.
The seven body rows are individual items with no declared groups or subtotal rows.
keep_whole: Part numbers, package codes, supplier names and numerical values with their units where possible.
Technical identifiers such as ARM Cortex-M3 and specification units such as 10 kΩ, 72 MHz and 2.54 mm where space permits.
may_wrap: Descriptions can wrap between phrases and specification items.
Multiword headers and supplier names can wrap at word boundaries when needed.
same_scale: Quantity and unit price should remain compact relative to the descriptive fields.
Part number and supplier need enough width for their identifiers; description benefits from substantially more flexible space.
d3.h_vs_v: At 360px, fitting all five columns forces breaks within some identifiers and supplier names and produces tall rows. Scrolling can preserve those units and give descriptions natural line breaks, at the cost of moving horizontally between identification and purchasing fields.

analysis.strengths: Part numbers, prices and suppliers stay whole; descriptions take at most two lines, and the equal-height data rows create a steady lookup rhythm.
analysis.faults: The table requires substantial horizontal scrolling. The first viewport shows complete part numbers but only fragments of descriptions, with quantity, price and supplier offscreen. The break between 5.25 and V separates a measurement.
analysis.spatial_logic: It reserves the minimum practical widths for identifiers, quantity and supplier, protects the price, and gives the remaining space to descriptions.

analysis.strengths: All five columns are present in the viewport, and complete prices remain easy to compare.
analysis.faults: Part numbers, supplier names, the Description and Supplier headers, and many description words break internally. Tall rows and fragmented text make lookup and continuous reading difficult.
analysis.spatial_logic: It protects quantity and price while distributing the remaining width among part number, description and a particularly narrow supplier column.

analysis.strengths: All columns are legible in the full table, descriptions take at most two lines, and uniform data-row heights support scanning. Its extra description width keeps 5.25 V together.
analysis.faults: It requires the most horizontal scrolling, while the extra width does not reduce row heights relative to P. The viewport still cuts descriptions and hides the three rightmost columns; 0603 is stranded on a line in one row.
analysis.spatial_logic: It uses the same protected widths as P and gives description another 20 px to improve some line breaks.

analysis.strengths: Identifiers, prices and suppliers remain whole, and it is 50 px narrower than P. Most descriptions fit on two lines.
analysis.faults: The microcontroller row takes three lines and separates 20 KB from RAM; 2-line also breaks across lines. The initial viewport still shows only part numbers and partial descriptions.
analysis.spatial_logic: It reduces the description column while preserving the widths needed by the other fields, accepting one taller row to reduce scrolling.

analysis.strengths: All columns appear at once. The extra part-number and supplier space reduces some fragmentation compared with Q, and the header is shorter.
analysis.faults: Several prices break within the amount, making financial comparison particularly difficult. Identifiers, supplier names and descriptions also fragment, producing very tall rows.
analysis.spatial_logic: It shifts width from price to part number, description and supplier, trading intact prices for somewhat less fragmentation elsewhere.

analysis.strengths: It is the narrowest scrolling candidate, preserves identifiers, prices and supplier names, and has the same row heights as S.
analysis.faults: Its microcontroller description splits Cortex-M3 across lines, as well as separating 20 from KB flash. The initial viewport still cuts descriptions and hides quantity, price and supplier.
analysis.spatial_logic: It takes another 10 px from S's description column to reduce scrolling, at the cost of less natural technical line breaks.

rounds.insights: The content cannot keep all long identifiers, supplier names, prices and useful description phrases whole within 360 px: their measured minimum widths already exceed the viewport before description space is added. Scrolling preserves the table's lookup function much better, though the first view cannot show every field. Among the scrolling layouts, description width controls both the travel distance and the quality of technical line breaks; the shortest table is not automatically the easiest to read. Among fitting layouts, preserving complete prices is a better use of space than the allocation in T, but substantial fragmentation remains unavoidable.

analysis.strengths: Complete part numbers and suppliers are easy to scan, and descriptions fit in two lines without breaking words. Consistent row heights support comparison.
analysis.faults: The table requires substantial horizontal scrolling. The initial viewport shows complete part numbers but only fragments of descriptions, with quantity, price and supplier out of sight.
analysis.spatial_logic: The generous description width creates an even, compact grid, though it separates identifiers from purchasing details across a wide table.

analysis.strengths: Quantity and price remain legible, and almost the entire table width lies within the viewport.
analysis.faults: Part numbers, descriptions and especially suppliers break within words. The supplier header becomes nearly vertical, and the slight horizontal overflow still requires scrolling. Tall rows make lookup and comparison arduous.
analysis.spatial_logic: A few pixels saved in width impose extreme height and fragmentation, with large empty areas beside the longest wrapped cells.

analysis.strengths: Like s0A, it preserves identifiers and suppliers, keeps descriptions to two lines and gives the rows a steady rhythm. It is slightly narrower.
analysis.faults: The description wraps some units awkwardly, including separating 72 from MHz and 5.25 from V. Purchasing columns remain beyond the initial viewport.
analysis.spatial_logic: Its compact, uniform rows are useful for comparison, but the narrower description saves little scrolling relative to s0A and produces less natural breaks.

analysis.strengths: It reduces horizontal travel while retaining whole identifiers and supplier names. Most descriptions remain within two lines.
analysis.faults: The microcontroller row grows to three lines and separates 20 KB from RAM; other breaks also interrupt technical phrases. The initial viewport still hides the purchasing columns.
analysis.spatial_logic: A narrower description trades some vertical regularity for reduced width. The one taller row is acceptable if the shorter horizontal journey is valued.

analysis.strengths: All five columns are accessible without horizontal scrolling, and quantities and prices remain readable.
analysis.faults: Part numbers and supplier names fragment across lines, as do words in the description and headers. Tall, uneven rows make it difficult to scan a BOM or associate purchasing details with an identifier.
analysis.spatial_logic: The fit is achieved by compressing the text-bearing columns below their content needs, producing a long table with considerable empty space in the numeric columns.

rounds.insights: This BOM needs intact part numbers for reliable lookup and enough description width for technical phrases. The scrolling layouts preserve those functions much better, but their first viewport exposes only part of the description and none of the purchasing columns. A viewport-fitting layout cannot accommodate every longest unbreakable unit: the measured minima plus padding already exceed the available width. Within that constraint, width should be assigned deliberately to the most important lookup fields and to avoiding the worst word fragmentation.

analysis.strengths: Quantity and complete prices are visible at first sight, with the supplier column immediately to the right. The full table preserves the grid and all content.
analysis.faults: Part numbers, descriptions and supplier names break inside words or identifiers. Long rows make cross-column lookup slow, and the supplier requires scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow first two columns bring prices into the initial viewport, but that gain comes at the cost of fragmented text and a very tall table.

analysis.strengths: More room for part numbers and descriptions reduces fragmentation and height compared with s1B. Quantity remains fully visible initially.
analysis.faults: Several identifiers and supplier names still split, and the initial viewport cuts through prices while hiding suppliers.
analysis.spatial_logic: The extra width improves reading within the first columns, but shifts the price column across the viewport edge, weakening the initial view for purchasing tasks.

analysis.strengths: Identifiers, supplier names and prices remain whole. Descriptions wrap naturally, headers fit on one line, and the consistent two-line data rows make scanning and comparison easy in the full table.
analysis.faults: The first viewport contains complete part numbers but only part of each description; quantity, price and supplier all require substantial horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: Generous description width creates a compact, orderly table vertically, while spreading related purchasing fields far apart horizontally.

analysis.strengths: All five columns are present within the viewport, and quantities and prices remain legible.
analysis.faults: Headers, part numbers, descriptions and suppliers fragment severely, including supplier names broken into tiny pieces. The resulting tall rows make lookup and comparison difficult.
analysis.spatial_logic: Fitting every column forces the available width below the content's practical minimum, producing an uneven and extremely tall grid.

rounds.insights: The full-width s0A best preserves the units needed for a BOM: exact part numbers, readable specifications, prices and supplier names. Its main cost is horizontal travel. The intermediate layouts reduce that travel but still fracture important text; s1C also places prices across the initial viewport edge. A fitted layout inevitably sacrifices some whole identifiers or names, so its widths should distribute that damage deliberately rather than reduce the supplier to a narrow strip.

analysis.strengths: Quantity and prices remain easy to scan, and the description column preserves more words than in Q.
analysis.faults: The supplier column is almost unusable: names and the header break into tiny fragments, making it the main cause of extreme row heights. Part numbers and some description words also split. The layout still requires horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: A small saving in horizontal space produces a very tall table with large empty areas beneath the short quantity and price values.

analysis.strengths: Part numbers, supplier names, prices and headers remain whole. Descriptions wrap naturally into at most two lines, and consistent row heights make comparison straightforward.
analysis.faults: The initial phone view shows part numbers and only part of each description; quantity, price and supplier require substantial horizontal scrolling. Associating those fields with a part requires tracking across a wide row.
analysis.spatial_logic: Width is assigned according to content needs, producing a compact and orderly table vertically, at the cost of a wide horizontal reading path.

analysis.strengths: All five columns are present in the viewport, and quantities and prices remain legible.
analysis.faults: Part numbers, supplier names, description words and several headers split unnaturally. The fragmented identifiers make lookup difficult, while tall rows and empty numeric cells slow comparison.
analysis.spatial_logic: Keeping every column visible distributes an insufficient width across too many competing text fields. The resulting vertical expansion outweighs the benefit of seeing the entire grid at once.

rounds.insights: This BOM depends on accurate part-number lookup and readable supplier names, both of which need more width than a five-column phone viewport can provide. Scrolling can preserve those units, but a narrower scrolling layout may reduce travel at the cost of more description lines. A fitted layout necessarily fragments some content; its best allocation should protect identifiers and numeric values as far as possible while keeping descriptions and suppliers usable.

bad.why: Part numbers, supplier names and several prices break across lines. Split prices are especially hard to scan and compare.
The extremely narrow supplier column fragments names into tiny pieces and drives excessive row heights, yet the table still requires horizontal scrolling.

contrast.why: Near-equal widths fit the viewport but give unnecessary space to quantity while splitting part numbers, prices, supplier names and descriptions. Equal treatment ignores their different content and lookup roles.

sameFunctionGroups.why: Both contain numerical values, but quantities are short counts and prices need room for currency and decimal precision. Their widths should reflect those different requirements.

synthesis.rationale: Layout P keeps part numbers, prices and supplier names whole and gives every description two lines, with slightly less horizontal travel than the similarly compact s0A and R. Layout Q is the stronger fitting candidate because it preserves prices on one line, but it severely fragments part numbers, descriptions and supplier names; it is a conditional finalist only to represent the required no-scroll class, not a layout I would publish without reservation. In the scrolling layouts, the initial viewport shows part numbers and only part of the descriptions, so readers must scroll to reach quantities, prices and suppliers.

general: Protect identifiers and numeric values from internal line breaks when they are used for lookup or comparison.
Allocate width according to content and reading task, and judge the initial viewport as well as the complete table.
Compare wrapping and scrolling together: a narrower table can demand substantially more vertical reading.
specific: A 186 px part-number column and a 154 px supplier column accommodate the longest unbreakable entries in this BOM.
A 300 px description column gives every row in Layout P two lines while retaining compact, consistent row heights.
Neither fitting candidate preserves all important semantic units at this viewport and font size.

synthesis.tradeoffs: Layout P requires substantial horizontal scrolling and hides three columns initially. Layout Q avoids horizontal scrolling but is much taller and forces disruptive breaks throughout the table. Layout S reduces horizontal travel compared with P but gives the microcontroller description a third line.
synthesis.uncertain: The best scrolling width depends on whether readers prioritize shorter vertical scanning or less horizontal travel. The supplied renders do not establish whether the surrounding interface makes horizontal scrolling discoverable.

critique.good: All five fields are visible together without horizontal scrolling, and quantities remain easy to scan.
critique.problems: Part numbers, prices, supplier names and even the Unit price header break across lines. Descriptions are fragmented, rows are very tall, and the dense vertical text makes cross-row comparison difficult.
critique.cause: The 100 px part-number, 105 px description, 53 px price and 54 px supplier columns are too narrow for their contents; the 47 px quantity column is adequate.

critique.good: Part numbers, prices and supplier names remain whole. The compact purchasing columns and two- or three-line descriptions make the full table reasonably balanced and scannable.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the description and hides all purchasing fields. Some technical units wrap at awkward points, such as SOT-23-6, and the varied row heights slow scanning somewhat.
critique.cause: The 186 px identifier and 220 px description columns already exceed the viewport together. The description width is a compromise: it limits scrolling but forces several lines in longer descriptions.

critique.good: Every cell fits on one line, producing compact, uniform rows and making individual values easy to read in the full table.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows only part numbers and the beginning of descriptions. Reaching quantities, prices and suppliers requires substantial horizontal travel, making it harder to relate purchasing details back to identifiers.
critique.cause: The 547 px description column preserves every description on one line but pushes the purchasing columns far to the right; the other columns are appropriately sized.

critique.good: Quantities and prices remain intact, and all five fields are visible without scrolling.
critique.problems: Supplier names fragment into near-vertical strings, descriptions and identifiers break inside words, and the resulting tall rows make comparison laborious. The supplier header also dominates the header height.
critique.cause: The 39px supplier column and 83px description column are especially restrictive; 110px is also too narrow for the longest part numbers.

critique.good: Part numbers, prices and suppliers remain whole, descriptions use at most two lines, and the regular row heights make the full table easy to scan.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows only part numbers and a portion of each description; purchasing fields require substantial horizontal scrolling. Some description lines break between a number and its unit.
critique.cause: The 186px identifier and 300px description columns place quantity 486px from the table’s left edge; the generous description width also makes the table 779px wide.

critique.good: Identifiers, prices and supplier names stay whole, while the narrower description reduces horizontal travel compared with d1r1B. Headers remain on one line.
critique.problems: Several descriptions take three lines, with uneven row heights and some awkward breaks in specifications, including SOT-23-6. The initial viewport still hides all purchasing fields.
critique.cause: The 220px description column trades 80px of width for additional wrapping; together with the 186px identifier column, it places quantity beyond the initial viewport.

critique.good: All fields are initially visible, and the wider description and supplier columns make it substantially shorter and more usable than d1r1A. Quantities remain intact.
critique.problems: Part numbers, prices and supplier names split inside their values, making exact lookup and purchasing comparisons difficult. Several descriptions and headers also break awkwardly.
critique.cause: The 100px part-number, 53px price and 54px supplier columns are too narrow for their content; the 105px description column also forces some word breaks.

critique.good: All five fields are visible together, and quantities and prices remain intact.
critique.problems: Identifiers, descriptions and supplier names fragment heavily. The tall rows make it difficult to scan across components, and several headers break awkwardly.
critique.cause: The 90 px part-number and 92 px description columns force breaks inside words and identifiers; the 50 px supplier column is especially restrictive. The 80 px price column preserves prices but leaves little room for the other fields.

critique.good: Part numbers, prices and supplier names stay whole. Descriptions are readable in mostly two lines, with a compact, orderly row rhythm.
critique.problems: The microcontroller description takes three lines, and the initial viewport shows only part of the description; purchasing fields require horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 260 px description column is slightly too narrow for the longest description in two lines, while the combined 739 px table width places the last three columns beyond the initial viewport.

critique.good: The initial viewport shows complete part numbers, descriptions and quantities. Prices and supplier names also remain whole when scrolled into view.
critique.problems: Descriptions become narrow stacks, with technical phrases such as Cortex-M3 and SOT-23-6 split across lines. Tall rows create large empty areas in the surrounding columns and slow comparison.
critique.cause: The 128 px description column makes room for quantity in the initial viewport but forces four to six lines in many descriptions.

critique.good: All descriptions fit in two lines, creating consistent, compact rows. Identifiers, prices and suppliers remain whole, and the full table is easy to scan.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows complete identifiers but only fragments of descriptions; quantity, price and supplier require substantial horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 300 px description column supports an even row rhythm but brings the total width to 779 px.

critique.good: All fields appear together, the description header fits on one line, and the table is shorter than d1r2A.
critique.problems: Part numbers, supplier names and prices break across lines, making exact lookup and price comparison difficult. Descriptions also contain awkward breaks, and the price header splits within a word.
critique.cause: The 100 px part-number, 105 px description, 53 px price and 54 px supplier columns are all too narrow for important content.

critique.good: Quantities and prices remain readable, and the part numbers are more legible than the supplier names.
critique.problems: Supplier names and their header fragment into near-vertical text, dominating row heights. Part numbers and description words also split. The table still requires a small horizontal scroll.
critique.cause: The 38 px supplier column is far too narrow; the 100 px part number and description columns also force breaks inside identifiers and words.

critique.good: The wider part number column keeps more of each identifier together, and quantities remain easy to scan.
critique.problems: Supplier names fragment severely, prices split across lines, and description words break. Tall rows make comparison laborious, while the table still slightly exceeds the viewport.
critique.cause: The 38 px supplier and 55 px price columns are too narrow; shifting space to the 130 px part number column also leaves only 95 px for descriptions.

critique.good: Identifiers, prices and supplier names stay whole. Descriptions wrap without breaking words, and the compact purchasing columns scan clearly.
critique.problems: Descriptions occupy up to four lines, with some values separated from their units. The initial viewport cuts through the description and hides all purchasing fields.
critique.cause: The 195 px description column limits natural grouping; the 186 px identifier column and total table width put the later columns beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Whole identifiers and supplier names, two-line descriptions and uniform body rows make the complete table easy to scan and compare.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through descriptions and hides the purchasing fields. Reaching the supplier requires substantial horizontal scrolling; a few specifications still wrap between a number and its unit.
critique.cause: The 300 px description column improves vertical reading but pushes the quantity, price and supplier columns farther to the right.

critique.good: All five fields are visible together, quantities and prices remain intact, and the supplier column is less severely compressed than in d1r3A and d1r3B.
critique.problems: Part numbers, description words and supplier names break unnaturally. The tall, uneven rows slow lookup and make the table visually crowded.
critique.cause: The 90 px part number, 92 px description and 50 px supplier columns cannot accommodate their longer unbreakable content within the viewport.

critique.good: Part numbers, prices and suppliers remain whole; all headers fit on one line. The complete description column is initially visible.
critique.problems: Descriptions form tall, narrow blocks, with specification values sometimes separated across lines. Rows have uneven heights and substantial empty space in the purchasing columns. Quantity is cut by the initial viewport edge.
critique.cause: The 150px description column drives wrapping and row height; the first three columns together extend just beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Descriptions are much easier to read, identifiers and purchasing fields stay whole, and most rows have a consistent two-line height.
critique.problems: The microcontroller description takes three lines, and the initial viewport cuts through every description while hiding all purchasing fields. Reading across a row requires substantial horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 250px description column improves vertical rhythm but, after the 186px identifier column, extends well beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Quantities and prices remain readable, and the table requires only a small horizontal scroll.
critique.problems: Supplier names and their header fragment into almost vertical strings; part numbers and description words also split. The resulting tall, uneven rows make lookup and comparison difficult, while scrolling is still required.
critique.cause: The 38px supplier column is severely undersized; the 105px identifier and 110px description columns also cannot hold their longest unbreakable content.

critique.good: Every description fits in two lines, producing a calm, consistent row rhythm. Part numbers, prices and suppliers remain whole, and all headers are on one line.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the descriptions and hides quantity, price and supplier. The wide table requires considerable scrolling to connect identifiers with purchasing fields.
critique.cause: The 300px description column gives excellent vertical economy but pushes the purchasing columns farther to the right.

critique.good: All five columns are visible together, and quantities and prices remain whole. This makes the purchasing fields accessible without horizontal scrolling.
critique.problems: Long part numbers, supplier names and description words break arbitrarily; even two headers split within words. Tall rows and fragmented text make identifiers and specifications hard to scan.
critique.cause: The 90px identifier, 92px description and 50px supplier columns are too narrow for their content. The 80px price column preserves price values but makes the header wrap.

critique.good: All five fields are visible at once, and the quantity column remains compact and readable.
critique.problems: Part numbers, prices, supplier names and some description words break across lines. The fragmented headers and tall rows make lookup and comparison laborious.
critique.cause: The 95 px part-number, 112 px description, 55 px price and 50 px supplier columns are all too narrow for important content.

critique.good: Identifiers, prices and supplier names remain whole, while descriptions mostly wrap into manageable two- or three-line blocks. The full table has clear row groupings and a useful balance of width and height.

contrast.idea: Near-equal widths fit the viewport but give unnecessary space to quantity while splitting part numbers, prices, supplier names and descriptions. Equal treatment ignores their different content and lookup roles.

d1r1B.why: Identifiers stay whole and the consistently two-line descriptions make rows easy to scan. The initial viewport cuts through descriptions and leaves quantity, price and supplier offscreen; a few values and units also fall on separate lines.

d3r1C.why: Most descriptions occupy two lines and the compact rows scan well, but Cortex-M3 breaks at the hyphen and the longest description needs three lines. The first viewport cuts through descriptions and hides the remaining columns.

d2r2B.why: Cortex-M3 stays together, improving on B, while most rows remain compact. The microcontroller description still runs to three lines, and the initial viewport cuts through the description column.

vc_pref.why: The initial view contains complete part numbers and descriptions, making identification practical before scrolling. Narrow descriptions create three- and four-line rows and separate some values from their units; quantity, price and supplier remain offscreen.

d1r2A.why: All columns are visible and prices stay whole, but part numbers, supplier names and even headers fragment across lines. Tall rows and a very narrow supplier column make lookup and continuous reading difficult.

contrast.why: Equal widths give excess space to quantity while splitting part numbers, prices, descriptions and supplier names. The resulting long rows make even a short BOM laborious to scan.

ref_equal.why: Like F, this fragments identifiers, prices and ordinary words while leaving unused space in quantity cells. Its slightly narrower columns produce still more wrapping and a taller table.

ref_auto.why: Part number, description and quantity are visible together initially, and identifiers and prices remain whole. The narrow description column breaks technical phrases across many short lines, producing tall rows and substantial empty space in neighboring cells.

d1r1B.why: The full table has consistently two-line descriptions and an even row rhythm. Its greater width puts more of each description and all quantity, price and supplier data beyond the initial viewport, increasing horizontal travel.

d1r1B.why: Descriptions fit in two lines and the uniform row heights make scanning easy; identifiers and purchasing fields remain intact. Its greater width requires substantial horizontal travel, and the first view cuts through descriptions.

ref_auto.why: Part number, description and quantity appear together initially, and the remaining columns require less scrolling. Narrow descriptions produce up to six lines and split technical designations; the price header also wraps.
